etymology: Mary Stuart (1542-1587), the Roman Catholic Queen of Scotland whose reign coincided with the Scottish Reformation and whose contest with John Knox marked the conflict of crown and Kirk.
biblical_def: Mary, Queen of Scots (Mary Stuart, 1542-1587) was the Roman Catholic Queen of Scotland whose reign (1561-1567) coincided with the triumph of the Scottish Reformation, and whose contest with John Knox and the Reformed Kirk became a defining drama of crown against gospel. Returning from France a devout Catholic to a newly Protestant realm, Mary sought to maintain her Mass and her religion against the Reformation that Parliament had established. Knox confronted her with a boldness that has become famous, refusing to flatter the throne and insisting that subjects owe obedience to God above the commands of princes—for we ought to obey God rather than men. Her reign collapsed amid intrigue, murder, and scandal; she was forced to abdicate, fled to England, was held prisoner by Elizabeth for nineteen years, and was at last executed in 1587 for her part in plots against the English crown. The dictionary treats Mary not as a figure to be either romanticized or vilified, but as a sober case in the providence of God and the relation of conscience to authority. Two truths it holds together. First, the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD; God changeth the times and seasons, removeth kings and setteth up kings, and He overruled the contest of Mary and Knox for the establishing of the gospel in Scotland. Second, Knox's stand teaches the limits of obedience to rulers: subjects honour the magistrate, but when the magistrate commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands, they must obey God rather than men. The dictionary thus reads Mary's reign as a witness to the sovereignty of God over thrones and to the duty of conscience bound by the Word of God above the will of any earthly sovereign.
webster_summary: Mary Stuart (1542-1587), the Roman Catholic Queen of Scotland whose reign clashed with John Knox and the Reformed Kirk; a case in the sovereignty of God over thrones and the duty to obey God rather than men.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the romanticizing or vilifying of Mary that obscures the lesson of God's sovereignty over thrones and the limits of obedience to rulers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Popular history romanticizes Mary as a tragic, wronged heroine or vilifies her as a scheming villainess, and in either case loses the lesson her reign teaches. The dictionary reads her soberly within the providence of God. The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, who turneth it whithersoever He will; God changeth the times and seasons and removeth and setteth up kings. The contest between the Catholic queen and the Reformed Kirk, with all its intrigue and tragedy, God overruled for the establishing of His gospel in Scotland. The throne did not master the Word; the Word, by God's sovereignty, outlasted the throne.

Mary's reign also illumines the relation of conscience to authority. Knox honoured the office of the queen yet refused to flatter her sin or surrender the gospel to her will, standing on the principle that we ought to obey God rather than men. The dictionary holds the balance Scripture teaches: subjects owe real honour and obedience to the civil magistrate, yet that obedience has a limit, for when the ruler commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands, the conscience bound by the Word must obey God first. Mary, Queen of Scots, stands as a witness both to the sovereignty of God over the thrones of the earth and to the liberty of a conscience captive to the Word of God.

etymology: From “Reformed” (of the Reformed/Calvinistic tradition) and “Baptists”; the confessional tradition holding Reformed doctrine together with believers' baptism, anchored in the 1689 London Baptist Confession.
biblical_def: Reformed Baptists are the confessional tradition that holds the doctrines of the Reformed faith—the five solas, the sovereignty of God in salvation, the doctrines of grace—together with the conviction that baptism belongs to believers only, by immersion, as the New Testament pattern. They are the heirs of the Particular Baptists of seventeenth-century England, whose 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith (closely following the Westminster Confession, but differing on baptism, the church, and the civil magistrate) is the dictionary's own primary subordinate standard. The Reformed Baptist holds, with all the Reformed, that God chose His people in Christ before the foundation of the world, that salvation is by grace alone through faith alone, and that He keeps His own to the end. But on baptism he reads the New Testament to teach that the ordinance follows faith: the eunuch was baptized upon confessing that he believed with all his heart; we are buried with Christ by baptism into death, that we should walk in newness of life; he that believeth and is baptized shall be saved. Hence the Reformed Baptist baptizes believers, not infants, and holds the local church to be a gathered company of professing believers. The dictionary, standing in this tradition, marks Reformed Baptists against two misunderstandings: that they are mere Calvinistic versions of revivalist or Arminian Baptists (they are confessional and covenantal, not individualistic), and that their difference from Presbyterians on baptism divides them in the gospel (it does not; they are one with their paedobaptist brethren in the doctrines of grace, differing as friends on the subjects of baptism and church government). The Reformed Baptist tradition is the dictionary's home: Reformed in doctrine, Baptist in the ordinances, confessional in the line of 1689.
webster_summary: The confessional tradition holding Reformed doctrine with believers' baptism, anchored in the 1689 London Baptist Confession; the dictionary's own home—Reformed in the doctrines of grace, Baptist in the ordinances, one with paedobaptist brethren in the gospel.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the misunderstandings to correct are that Reformed Baptists are mere Calvinistic revivalists, and that their difference from Presbyterians on baptism divides them in the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two misunderstandings are worth correcting. The first supposes Reformed Baptists to be merely Calvinistic versions of revivalist or Arminian Baptists—individualistic, anti-confessional, suspicious of doctrine. The dictionary, standing in this tradition, answers that Reformed Baptists are confessional and covenantal, anchored in the 1689 London Baptist Confession, holding the whole Reformed system of doctrine: total depravity, unconditional election, definite atonement, effectual calling, and perseverance, with the five solas and the regulative principle of worship. They are not doctrinal minimalists but confessors of a full and historic faith.

The second misunderstanding makes the difference from Presbyterians on baptism a division in the gospel. It is not. Reformed Baptists and paedobaptist Presbyterians and Reformed are one in the doctrines of grace, the five solas, and the sovereignty of God in salvation; they differ as brethren on the subjects of baptism (believers only, by immersion) and on church government (congregational rather than presbyterian). The dictionary holds this difference to be real and worth contending for, yet within the household of faith. The Reformed Baptist tradition is the dictionary's own home—Reformed in doctrine, Baptist in the ordinances, confessional in the line of 1689—and it confesses the same gospel of free and sovereign grace as all the Reformed.

etymology: From “reconstruction” (a rebuilding); the twentieth-century theonomic and postmillennial movement led by R. J. Rushdoony and Greg Bahnsen, seeking to reconstruct society on the law of God.
biblical_def: Christian Reconstructionism is the twentieth-century movement, led chiefly by R. J. Rushdoony and Greg Bahnsen, that sought the reconstruction of society and the state upon the law of God, combining theonomy (the abiding authority of the Mosaic civil law), postmillennialism (the expectation that the gospel will triumph in history before Christ's return), and a strongly Calvinistic, presuppositional theology. The dictionary treats it with discriminating respect as a movement arising from within the Reformed family, holding genuine truths while pressing them, in the dictionary's judgment, to debatable and sometimes erroneous conclusions. Its commendable instincts are real: that the law of the LORD is perfect and good if used lawfully; that Christ did not come to destroy the law but to fulfil it; that His government and its increase shall have no end; and that the lordship of Christ extends over every sphere, including the civil. Against the privatizing of faith and the antinomian disregard of God's law, Reconstructionism rightly insisted that God's standards are not abolished and that society is accountable to its Maker. Yet the dictionary marks its errors and excesses. Its theonomy presses the abiding force of the Mosaic civil and penal code (including its capital sanctions) in a way the 1689 Confession does not, which teaches that the judicial laws of Israel expired with that state, binding now only so far as their general equity requires. Its postmillennial triumphalism can breed an over-realized expectation of cultural dominion. And in some hands it tended toward a coercive vision at odds with liberty of conscience. The dictionary commends the lordship of Christ over all of life and the goodness of God's law, while reading the theonomic and postmillennial claims through the corrective of the Confession and the New Testament's teaching that Christ's kingdom advances by Word and Spirit, not by the imposition of the Mosaic state.
webster_summary: The 20th-century theonomic, postmillennial movement (Rushdoony, Bahnsen) seeking to reconstruct society on God's law; commended for the lordship of Christ and the goodness of the law, yet corrected on the abiding force of the Mosaic civil code and its triumphalism.

corruption_summary: Reconstructionism rightly holds the goodness of the law and Christ's lordship, but errs in pressing the Mosaic civil and penal code as abiding, and in a postmillennial triumphalism that can over-realize cultural dominion.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary commends the genuine truths Christian Reconstructionism recovered against the spirit of the age. Its presuppositional defence of the faith, its insistence on the goodness and abiding relevance of God's law (the law is good if a man use it lawfully), its confession that Christ came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it, and its proclamation of the lordship of Christ over every sphere of life stand against the privatizing of faith, the antinomian contempt for God's standards, and the secular myth of a neutral public square. In an age that would shut Christ out of law and culture, Reconstructionism rightly insisted that the increase of His government has no end.

Yet the dictionary names its errors and excesses. Its theonomy presses the abiding authority of the Mosaic civil and penal code—including its capital sanctions—further than the 1689 Confession allows, which teaches that the judicial laws given to Israel as a body politic expired with that state and oblige now only so far as their general equity requires. Its postmillennial confidence can swell into a triumphalist expectation of cultural dominion that Scripture does not warrant, and in some hands its vision grew coercive, at odds with liberty of conscience. The dictionary therefore commends the lordship of Christ and the goodness of the law while reading the theonomic and postmillennial claims through the corrective of the Confession and the New Testament's teaching that Christ's kingdom advances by the Word and Spirit, not by reimposing the Mosaic state.

etymology: From the figure of seven “mountains” or spheres of culture; the dominionist teaching, associated with the New Apostolic Reformation, that the church must take control of seven spheres of society.
biblical_def: The Seven Mountains Mandate is a dominionist teaching, associated chiefly with the New Apostolic Reformation and the charismatic movement, that the church is called to take control of seven “mountains” or spheres of society—religion, family, education, government, media, arts and entertainment, and business—in order to establish the kingdom of God on earth and prepare the way for Christ's return. The dictionary rejects the mandate as a corruption of the doctrine of the kingdom of God and of the church's mission. The Lord Himself declared, “My kingdom is not of this world,” and that it cometh not with observation; it advances not by the seizing of cultural power but by the preaching of the gospel, the work of the Word and the Spirit—“not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.” The Seven Mountains scheme mistakes the nature of Christ's reign, confusing the spiritual advance of His kingdom through conversion and discipleship with a program of institutional conquest, and it tends to a triumphalism that promises what God has not promised. More gravely, in its appetite for the kingdoms and the glory of this world, it echoes the very temptation the Lord refused in the wilderness, when Satan offered Him all the kingdoms of the world and He answered, “Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.” The dictionary affirms that Christ is Lord over every sphere and that Christians are to be salt and light in all their callings, doing good in family, work, and society; but it denies that the church's mission is to seize the “mountains” of culture, and holds that the kingdom comes by the gospel, not by dominion, and will be consummated by the King Himself at His return, not built to completion by His servants' conquest of the world.
webster_summary: The dominionist teaching (linked to the New Apostolic Reformation) that the church must seize seven spheres of culture to build the kingdom; rejected as a corruption—Christ's kingdom is not of this world and advances by Word and Spirit, not cultural conquest.

corruption_summary: The Seven Mountains Mandate is itself the corruption: it mistakes Christ's spiritual kingdom for institutional conquest, breeds triumphalism, and in its appetite for worldly power echoes the temptation Christ refused.
corruption_paragraphs: The Seven Mountains Mandate is the corruption to be named, not a doctrine at risk of drift. It teaches that the church must seize control of the spheres of culture—government, media, business, and the rest—to build the kingdom of God on earth. But the Lord declared His kingdom not of this world, and said it comes not with observation but advances by the gospel, not by might nor power but by His Spirit. The mandate mistakes the very nature of Christ's reign, confusing the spiritual advance of His kingdom through conversion and discipleship with a program of institutional conquest, and so promises a dominion God has not promised to the church in this age.

More gravely, the appetite of the Seven Mountains teaching for the kingdoms and the glory of this world echoes the temptation the Lord Himself refused. When Satan offered Him all the kingdoms of the world, Christ answered, “Get thee hence, Satan… him only shalt thou serve.” The dictionary affirms what is true—that Christ is Lord over every sphere, and that Christians are to be salt and light, doing good in every lawful calling. But it denies that the church's mission is the conquest of the cultural “mountains.” The kingdom comes by the preaching of the gospel and the work of the Spirit, and it will be consummated not by the church's seizure of power but by the King Himself at His return.

etymology: A nineteenth-century American metaphysical movement teaching the creative power of the mind and positive thinking; a chief root of the prosperity gospel and word-of-faith teaching.
biblical_def: New Thought is a nineteenth-century American metaphysical and mind-cure movement, arising from the teaching of Phineas Quimby and spread through figures and groups such as Mary Baker Eddy's Christian Science, the Unity School, and the “positive thinking” popularizers, holding that the mind possesses creative power, that thoughts shape reality, that sickness and poverty arise from wrong thinking, and that man may attain health, wealth, and well-being by the right use of his mental and spiritual powers. The dictionary names New Thought as a serious corruption and, in its developed forms, a counterfeit religion. It denies the biblical doctrine of God, man, sin, and salvation, putting in the place of the sovereign Creator an impersonal divine principle, and in the place of the fallen sinner needing redemption a divine self needing only enlightenment. The apostle's warning fits it exactly: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men… and not after Christ”; for these are the vain babblings and oppositions of science falsely so called. New Thought exalts the thoughts of man, when the LORD declares, “My thoughts are not your thoughts.” The dictionary marks its lasting and dangerous legacy within the church: New Thought is a principal root of the prosperity gospel and the word-of-faith movement, which baptize its mind-power doctrine in Christian language—teaching that faith is a force, that positive confession creates reality, that the believer may command health and wealth by speaking the word. These the dictionary identifies as New Thought in Christian dress, corrupting the simplicity that is in Christ as the serpent beguiled Eve. Over against the whole system the dictionary holds the gospel: man is a fallen sinner, not a latent god; salvation is by the grace of God in Christ, not by the power of the mind; and reality is shaped not by human thought but by the Word of the God whose thoughts are higher than ours.
webster_summary: A 19th-century metaphysical movement (Quimby, Christian Science, “positive thinking”) teaching the creative power of the mind; a counterfeit religion and the chief root of the prosperity and word-of-faith gospels that dress its mind-power doctrine in Christian language.

corruption_summary: New Thought is itself the corruption: a counterfeit religion of mind-power that denies the biblical God, man, sin, and salvation, and whose Christianized offspring are the prosperity and word-of-faith gospels.
corruption_paragraphs: New Thought is the corruption to be named, not a doctrine at risk of drift. It is a metaphysical religion of mind-power, teaching that thoughts create reality, that the divine is an impersonal principle to be tapped, and that man attains health and wealth by right thinking. The dictionary names it a counterfeit of the faith. It replaces the sovereign personal God with a force, the fallen sinner with a latent god needing only enlightenment, and salvation by grace with self-improvement by mental technique. The apostle's words mark it exactly: it spoils men through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men and not after Christ, the vain babblings and oppositions of science falsely so called.

The dictionary presses especially its legacy within the professing church. New Thought is the principal root of the prosperity gospel and the word-of-faith movement, which take its mind-power doctrine and dress it in Christian language: faith becomes a creative force, “positive confession” becomes a means of commanding reality, and the believer is taught to speak health and wealth into being. The dictionary identifies these as New Thought in Christian clothing, corrupting the simplicity that is in Christ as the serpent beguiled Eve. Over against the whole scheme it sets the gospel: man is a sinner needing redemption, not a god needing enlightenment; salvation is by God's grace in Christ, not by the power of the mind; and the LORD's thoughts, not man's, govern reality, for His thoughts are not our thoughts.

etymology: From “hyper-” (excessive) and “charismatic” (of the spiritual gifts, Greek charismata); the extreme wing of the charismatic movement marked by unbridled claims of prophecy, miracle, and revelation.
biblical_def: “Hyper-charismatic” describes the extreme wing of the charismatic and Pentecostal movement, marked by unbridled and unaccountable claims of prophecy, miracle, new revelation, and apostolic authority—as in the New Apostolic Reformation, certain “signs and wonders” ministries, and movements such as Bethel and the Toronto phenomenon. The dictionary, holding the cessationist Reformed position, distinguishes this excess both from the historic Reformed faith and from the more sober charismatic believers who, though continuationist, hold to Scripture's authority and order. The marks of the hyper-charismatic are these: prophecies and “words from the Lord” that add to or rival Scripture and are seldom tested or held accountable when they fail; claims of miracles and healings unverified and often manifestly false; chaotic and ecstatic worship that the apostle's rule would forbid, for God is not the author of confusion but of peace; and self-styled apostles and prophets claiming an authority the closed canon does not allow. The dictionary marks the movement against the plain commands of Scripture. Believers are to try the spirits, whether they are of God, for many false prophets are gone out into the world; they are to beware of those who turn away their ears from the truth unto fables; and they are warned by the Lord that many will claim to have prophesied and done wonderful works in His name, to whom He will say, “I never knew you.” The dictionary does not deny the reality of the Spirit's work or counsel a dead formalism; it insists that the Spirit who inspired the Scriptures does not contradict or add to them, that all things in worship be done decently and in order, and that every claim to prophecy, miracle, and revelation be tested by the Word of God, the closed and sufficient canon.
webster_summary: The extreme wing of the charismatic movement, marked by unaccountable claims of prophecy, miracle, and new revelation (NAR, Bethel, Toronto); rejected for adding to Scripture and breeding confusion, against the commands to try the spirits and do all things in order.
webster_full: HYPER-CHARISMATIC, adjective. [Greek charismata, gifts.] The extreme, unaccountable wing of the charismatic movement.

Against the commands to try the spirits (1 John 4:1) and do all things in order (1 Corinthians 14:33).

corruption_summary: Hyper-charismatic excess is itself the corruption: it adds to Scripture by unaccountable prophecy, breeds confusion in worship, and exalts self-styled apostles and unverified miracles against the closed and sufficient canon.
corruption_paragraphs: The hyper-charismatic excess is the corruption to be named. It floods the church with prophecies and “words from the Lord” that add to or rival the closed canon and are rarely tested or repented of when they fail; it parades unverified and often manifestly false miracles; it fosters chaotic, ecstatic worship that the apostle's rule forbids, for God is not the author of confusion but of peace; and it raises up self-styled apostles and prophets claiming an authority that ended with the foundation-laying apostles. The dictionary, holding the cessationist position, names this a grave departure from Scripture's authority and order.

Yet the dictionary is careful in its distinctions. It does not equate every charismatic believer with the hyper-charismatic fringe; many continuationists hold to the authority of Scripture and the order of worship and are brethren in the gospel. Nor does it counsel a dead formalism that quenches the Spirit. Its insistence is this: the Spirit who inspired the Scriptures neither contradicts nor adds to them; believers are commanded to try the spirits, for many false prophets are gone out into the world; and the Lord Himself warned that many will boast of prophecies and wonders done in His name, to whom He will say, “I never knew you.” Every claim to prophecy, miracle, and revelation must be tested by the Word of God, the closed and all-sufficient canon, and all things in worship done decently and in order.
roots_summary: From “hyper-” (Greek, over, excessive) and “charismatic” (from charismata, gifts of grace); the excess of the charismatic movement beyond the bounds of Scripture and order.

She tried the spirits by the Word, refusing the unverified wonders paraded in Christ's name.

pos: noun phrase (a false teaching on sanctification)
etymology: From “carnal” (Latin carnalis, fleshly); the false teaching that posits a permanent class of saved-but-unsanctified “carnal Christians” living in unbroken worldliness.
biblical_def: The carnal Christian error is the false teaching that there exists a permanent and acceptable class of “carnal Christians”—persons truly saved who may live indefinitely in unbroken worldliness and sin, having received Christ as Saviour but not as Lord, and who differ from the “spiritual” Christian only in degree of blessing, not in the reality of regeneration. It often appeals to Paul's words to the Corinthians, “I could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, even as unto babes in Christ.” The dictionary rejects the error while acknowledging the grain of truth it abuses. The truth: genuine believers do remain in part carnal, struggling with indwelling sin, and may for a season be worldly and immature—Paul does call the Corinthians carnal. The error: turning this temporary and rebuked condition into a permanent, settled, acceptable category, so that a person may claim to be a Christian while showing no fruit, no growth, no struggle against sin, no submission to Christ's lordship. Scripture forbids this conclusion. If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature; old things are passed away. Faith without works is dead. He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar. The dictionary marks the error as a form of cheap grace and easy-believism that divorces saving faith from its fruit and Christ's saviourhood from His lordship—a division the Lordship-salvation controversy rightly resisted. True believers are sanctified, not merely justified; the grace that saves also transforms. A profession of faith joined to a settled, unbroken, unrepentant carnality is not the mark of a “carnal Christian” but the warning sign of a false profession. The dictionary holds that there is no permanent class of saved-but-unsanctified souls: the regenerate may stumble, but they do not finally and contentedly walk after the flesh, for they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh.
webster_summary: The false teaching of a permanent, acceptable class of saved-but-unsanctified “carnal Christians” living in unbroken sin; rejected as cheap grace divorcing faith from its fruit and Christ's saviourhood from His lordship (2 Corinthians 5:17; James 2:17).
webster_full: CARNAL CHRISTIAN ERROR, noun phrase. [Latin carnalis, fleshly.] The false teaching of a permanent class of saved-but-unsanctified Christians.
It posits believers who may live indefinitely in unbroken worldliness, having Christ as Saviour but not Lord.
It abuses Paul's rebuke of the carnal Corinthians (1 Corinthians 3:1).
Rejected: if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature (2 Corinthians 5:17); faith without works is dead.
A form of cheap grace divorcing faith from fruit and Christ's saviourhood from His lordship.
scriptures: And I, brethren, could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, even as unto babes in Christ.
Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
Jas 2:17

He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him.
corruption_summary: The carnal Christian error is itself the corruption: it turns a temporary, rebuked immaturity into a permanent acceptable class, divorcing saving faith from its fruit and Christ's saviourhood from His lordship.
corruption_paragraphs: The carnal Christian error is the corruption to be named, though it abuses a grain of truth. The truth is that genuine believers remain in part carnal, struggle with indwelling sin, and may for a season be worldly and immature; Paul indeed called the Corinthians carnal, even as babes in Christ. The error is to take this temporary and rebuked condition and harden it into a permanent, settled, acceptable category—a class of “carnal Christians” who may live indefinitely in unbroken sin, having received Christ as Saviour but never as Lord, differing from the spiritual only in reward. This the dictionary rejects as a form of cheap grace and easy-believism.

Scripture forbids the conclusion the error draws. If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature; old things are passed away. Faith without works is dead, being alone. He that saith he knows God and keeps not His commandments is a liar. The grace that justifies also sanctifies; there is no salvation that leaves a man unchanged, content in his sin, unsubmitted to Christ's lordship. The Lordship-salvation controversy rightly resisted this division of the Saviour from the Lord. The dictionary holds that a profession joined to a settled, unbroken, unrepentant carnality is not the badge of a lower class of Christian but the warning sign of a false profession; the regenerate may stumble, but they do not finally and contentedly walk after the flesh, for they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with its affections and lusts.
roots_summary: From the Latin carnalis (fleshly) and the Greek sarkikos (carnal, of the flesh); the error misreads Paul's temporary rebuke of carnal believers as a permanent category.
roots_lines: Carnalis, Latin, fleshly, from caro, flesh.
Sarkikos, Greek, carnal or fleshly, Paul's word for the Corinthians.
“Babes in Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:1) marks the condition as immature, not permanent.
Associated with the easy-believism the Lordship-salvation debate resisted.
Set against “a new creature” (2 Corinthians 5:17) and living faith (James 2:17).
usage: The pastor refuted the carnal Christian error, for the grace that justifies also sanctifies.
He warned that a settled, unrepentant carnality is the sign of a false profession, not a lower class of saint.
She held that the regenerate may stumble but do not finally walk content after the flesh.

pos: noun phrase (any counterfeit of the gospel)
etymology: From “false” and “gospel” (Old English godspel, good news); any counterfeit of the one true gospel of justification by grace through faith in Christ.
biblical_def: A false gospel is any counterfeit of the one true gospel of justification by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone—any message that, while perhaps using the name of Christ, in substance preaches another way of salvation. The apostle Paul names the danger in the sharpest terms: “I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel”; and he pronounces a double anathema upon any who pervert it: “If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed.” He warns of those who preach another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel, and unmasks them as false apostles, deceitful workers, transformed into apostles of Christ—no marvel, for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light. The dictionary holds that the test of a true gospel is not the use of Christian words but the substance of the message: whether salvation is by grace alone received by faith alone, or by some admixture of human works, merit, ritual, or power. By this test the dictionary names as false gospels the legalism of works-righteousness (including Rome's gospel of faith-plus-works anathematized at Trent); the prosperity gospel, which preaches health and wealth in place of Christ crucified; the liberal “social gospel” that replaces redemption from sin with social reform; the therapeutic gospel of self-esteem and self-fulfillment; and every scheme that adds to or subtracts from the finished work of Christ received by faith. The dictionary marks the gravity of the matter: a false gospel does not merely err on a secondary point but, in Paul's judgment, places its hearers under a curse, for it offers a salvation that cannot save. The remedy is to hold fast the gospel once delivered—Christ crucified and risen, righteousness imputed, salvation of free and sovereign grace—and to mark and avoid those who preach any other.
webster_summary: Any counterfeit of the true gospel of justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone; under Paul's anathema (Galatians 1:9), it includes works-righteousness, the prosperity gospel, the social gospel, and every scheme adding to or subtracting from Christ's finished work.
webster_full: FALSE GOSPEL, noun phrase. Any counterfeit of the true gospel of grace through faith in Christ.
Paul's anathema: “If any man preach any other gospel… let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:9).
Marked by “another Jesus… another spirit… another gospel” (2 Corinthians 11:4).
Its preachers are false apostles, Satan transformed into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14).
Includes works-righteousness, the prosperity gospel, the social gospel, and the therapeutic gospel.
scriptures: Ga 1:9
As we said before, so say I now again, If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed.
Ga 1:6
I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel:

For if he that cometh preacheth another Jesus, whom we have not preached, or if ye receive another spirit, which ye have not received, or another gospel, which ye have not accepted, ye might well bear with him.
And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.
corruption_summary: The false gospel is corruption itself: works-righteousness, the prosperity gospel, the social gospel, and the therapeutic gospel each offer a salvation that cannot save, and stand under the apostle's anathema.
corruption_paragraphs: The false gospel is the corruption itself, named and cursed by the apostle. Its test is not the use of Christian words—for it often comes clothed in the name of Christ, as Satan is transformed into an angel of light—but the substance of its message. The true gospel is salvation by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, His finished work received and His righteousness imputed. Any message that adds human works, merit, ritual, or power to that finished work, or substitutes some other benefit for it, is another gospel, and Paul pronounces a double anathema upon all who preach it.

The dictionary names the chief false gospels of the age and ages. The legalism of works-righteousness, including Rome's gospel of faith-plus-works anathematized at Trent, makes salvation partly earned. The prosperity gospel preaches health and wealth in the place of Christ crucified. The liberal social gospel replaces redemption from sin with social reform, and the therapeutic gospel replaces it with self-esteem and self-fulfillment. Each offers a salvation that cannot save, and so leaves its hearers under the curse. The dictionary's remedy is the apostle's: hold fast the gospel once delivered—Christ crucified and risen, righteousness imputed, salvation of free and sovereign grace—and mark and avoid those who preach any other, however plausible their words or transformed their appearance.
roots_summary: From “gospel” (Old English godspel, good news, rendering Greek euangelion); a “false” or “other” gospel (Greek heteron euangelion) under the apostolic anathema.
roots_lines: Euangelion, Greek, “good news,” the gospel; godspel, the Old English.
Heteron euangelion, Greek, “another gospel” of a different kind (Galatians 1:6).
Anathema, Greek, “accursed,” the apostolic sentence on false gospels.
Tested by substance—grace alone through faith alone—not by Christian words.
Satan “transformed into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14), the disguise of false gospels.
usage: The pastor tested every gospel by its substance, not its words, marking the false ones under Paul's anathema.
He named the prosperity gospel a false gospel that preaches gain in place of Christ crucified.
She held fast the gospel once delivered, marking and avoiding those who preached another.

etymology: Fuller Theological Seminary, founded in Pasadena in 1947 by Charles E. Fuller and Harold Ockenga as a flagship of the “new evangelicalism.”
biblical_def: Fuller Theological Seminary, founded in Pasadena, California, in 1947 by the radio evangelist Charles E. Fuller and the pastor Harold Ockenga, was established as a flagship academic institution of the “new evangelicalism,” intended to combine scholarly rigour with evangelical conviction and to engage the wider culture and academy. The dictionary treats Fuller as a sober and cautionary case-study in the doctrine of Scripture. At its founding the seminary stood for biblical inerrancy and orthodox evangelical faith, and gathered able defenders of it. But in the 1960s and 1970s Fuller became the centre of a painful controversy over inerrancy, and the institution revised its statement of faith to affirm the Bible's infallibility in matters of faith and practice while no longer affirming its full inerrancy in all that it touches—a decisive softening. The dictionary marks this as a grave landmark in the wider evangelical drift from the high doctrine of Scripture. The lesson is the apostle's charge: “Hold fast the form of sound words”; for a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump, and the removal of the ancient landmark which the fathers set leads further than the first step intends. When the foundation of a fully trustworthy Scripture is loosened, the structure built upon it is endangered, and the history of institutions that have abandoned inerrancy bears the warning out. The dictionary does not deny that godly men have taught and studied at Fuller, nor that good has been done there; it names the institutional trajectory as a warning, applying Paul's word to take heed unto oneself and unto the doctrine. Fuller stands as a reminder that orthodoxy is not inherited automatically but must be guarded in each generation, and that the surrender of inerrancy, however nuanced, is a breach in the wall that later generations pay for.
webster_summary: Fuller Theological Seminary (founded 1947), a flagship of the “new evangelicalism” that in the 1960s-70s softened its stand on biblical inerrancy; a cautionary case-study in the drift from the high doctrine of Scripture—a little leaven leavening the lump.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Fuller Seminary is itself a case-study of a corruption to be marked: the softening of the doctrine of Scripture. Founded for biblical inerrancy and orthodox evangelical conviction, the seminary in the 1960s and 1970s passed through a bitter controversy and revised its statement of faith, affirming the Bible's infallibility in matters of faith and practice while ceasing to affirm its full inerrancy in all that it touches. The lesson is the apostle's. “Hold fast the form of sound words”; a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump; remove not the ancient landmark which the fathers set. When the foundation of a fully trustworthy Scripture is loosened, the structure built upon it is endangered, and the trajectory of institutions that have abandoned inerrancy bears the warning out. etymology: Carl Ferdinand Howard Henry (1913-2003), American evangelical theologian, founding editor of Christianity Today, and author of God, Revelation and Authority.
biblical_def: Carl F. H. Henry (1913-2003) was an American evangelical theologian, journalist, and churchman, a leading architect of the mid-twentieth-century “new evangelicalism,” the founding editor of Christianity Today, and the author of the massive six-volume work God, Revelation and Authority, a sustained defence of the rationality of the Christian faith and the authority of God's propositional revelation in Scripture. The dictionary honours much in Henry's labour. Against the prevailing liberalism and neo-orthodoxy of his day, he defended the inspiration, inerrancy, and propositional truth of Scripture—that God has spoken truly and intelligibly, that the prophecy came not by the will of man but as holy men were moved by the Holy Ghost, that God's word is true from the beginning and shall stand for ever. He labored to give evangelicalism intellectual seriousness and to recall it to social as well as personal responsibility without surrendering the gospel. His high doctrine of Scripture and his defence of revealed truth against the irrationalism of neo-orthodoxy are a genuine service to the church. The dictionary, holding the Reformed and confessional faith, notes its differences and cautions. Henry was a broad evangelical, not a confessional Reformed theologian, and the “new evangelicalism” he helped lead, for all its strengths, opened doors—through its instinct for cultural engagement and cooperation—that later admitted the very compromises it meant to resist, as the trajectory of some of its institutions showed. The dictionary applies its rule: honour the genuine good—Henry's defence of biblical inerrancy and revealed, propositional truth, his intellectual seriousness, his stand against liberalism and neo-orthodoxy—while reading his broad-evangelical program through the corrective of the confessional Reformed tradition, which roots the defence of Scripture in the whole system of doctrine the great confessions set forth.
